evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 跟 as 从足、艮聲 and gives its original sense as the back of the foot/heel. It records the Shuowen alternative form 𣥦 as 从止、艮聲, noting 足 and 止 are semantically related shape elements. It supplies no oracle-bone or bronze examples for 跟, while listing one small-seal example; therefore the inspected entry does not establish a pre-imperial graphic chronology for 跟.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 跟

evidence.text: The database cites 焦氏易林《蹇之第三十九》, “頭痒搔跟” (itching head, scratch heel), as an early attested heel sense. The received text page inspected labels the work section but does not establish a date for this particular wording; it should not be dated from the web edition alone.

evidence.text: The inspected text has “頭痒搔跟，无益於疾” under the section titled 蹇之第三十九 (line item 49, 革). It verifies the wording in that received edition, but the page does not date the composition or prove the date at which this wording entered the text.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The entry traces object ‘bottom/back’ uses from heel, citing 清稗類鈔·鑒賞類 (“每冊之跟”), and gives shoe heel as a continuing use. It reports follow as a later common sense and quotes 正字通·足部, “俗謂隨行曰跟”; later cited examples include 三国演义 chapter 28 and 红楼梦 chapter 43. It then explains attendant/servant and marriage senses from follow, and later prepositional/object and conjunction uses with examples from 红楼梦, 老残游记, 龙须沟, and 小二黑结婚. These are the database’s reported citations, not independently dated first attestations of each extension.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 跟

evidence.source: 《重編國語辭典修訂本》, Taiwan Ministry of Education
evidence.text: The modern dictionary defines the noun as the back of a foot and heel of a shoe; the verb as going along or attending; and the preposition as ‘with/and’ or ‘to/toward’. It quotes the Qing-era novel 儒林外史 chapter 3 for following and 紅樓夢 chapter 43 for attending. This supplies attestations in named works but not composition or publication dates on the entry page.

evidence.field: 跟, 字形 and 語系
evidence.text: This reference also classifies 跟 as a phono-semantic graph with 艮 as sound element and gives heel, follow, and attach as glosses. Its account that 艮 signifies retreat due to an evil-eye taboo is a source-specific graphic/semantic interpretation, not confirmed by the other inspected evidence. It also reports that 釋名 associates 跟 with 木根 by resemblance; that is an ancient explanation, not proof that heel and root are historically cognate.
evidence.title: 跟とは？ 意味や使い方

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The entry transcribes the Shuowen explanation as “跟，足踵也。从足，艮聲。〔古痕切〕𣥦，跟或从止。” Thus Shuowen attributes heel as sense, 足 as semantic element and 艮 as phonetic element, and records 𣥦 with 止 as an alternative form. This is evidence for what the Han-period dictionary reports, not direct proof of the graph’s prehistoric formation.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 跟

evidence.text: The entry gives 艮 Old Chinese *kɯːns in its displayed reconstruction and identifies its rhyme group as 文. Its cross-system Middle Chinese comparison lists kən for Zhengzhang, Wang Li, Li Rong, Shao Rongfen, Pan Wuyun, and Pulleyblank; these are Middle Chinese values, not the displayed Old Chinese reconstruction.
evidence.title: 艮 - 字 - 上古音系 - 韻典網

evidence.field: Glyph origin / Zhengzhang 2003 sound series and readings
evidence.text: This entry identifies 跟 as an 艮-series phonetic graph and lists 跟 Old Chinese *kɯːn and 艮 *kɯːns in Zhengzhang (2003). It gives 跟 Middle Chinese fanqie 古痕切 and category 見開一痕平, with Mandarin gēn and Cantonese gan1; it gives 艮 Mandarin readings gèn, gěn (among others) and Cantonese gan3. In the stated reconstruction, the related initial and rhyme support a phonetic role despite the departing tone suffix on 艮. The source also reports 跟 as cognate with 根 (Old Chinese *kɯːn), attributed to Wang (1982), but no primary text supporting that cognacy was inspected here.
evidence.title: 跟 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.text: For 艮 the displayed Old Chinese form is *kɯːns; its table supplies Middle Chinese kən in the named reconstruction systems. Compared with 跟’s Zhengzhang *kɯːn and Middle Chinese kon in Baxter notation, this supports historical sound similarity for 艮 as a phonetic component. It does not establish the pronunciation of any depicted object or imply a whole-graph phonetic loan.
evidence.title: 艮 - 字 - 上古音系 - 韻典網

evidence.text: The character page labels 足 the meaning component and 艮 the sound component, displays a small-seal Shuowen form and modern regular form, and paraphrases Shuowen as 足踵也 with an alternative from 止. This broadly agrees with Shuowen and the CUHK analysis, but is not independent paleographic corroboration.

CUHK page is accessible and states no oracle or bronze examples in its entry but does give one small-seal example. The initially searched CUHK guide page was not used for character-specific evidence.

search_audit.query: 跟 足踵 焦氏易林 蹇之第三十九 日期; 跟 正字通 俗謂隨行曰跟 原文; 跟 甲骨 金文 字形 小篆 𣥦; 艮 鄭張 上古音 *kɯːns 根 跟 *kɯːn
search_audit.outcome: Inspected the 艮 entry in 韻典網, the Chinese Wiktionary 艮 entry, and the received 焦氏易林 text. Found the cited phrase 頭痒搔跟 and sound comparisons. No independently verified date for the wording or underlying composition was found.

gaps: No dated oracle-bone, bronze, or excavated manuscript attestation of 跟 was located. The consulted CUHK entry lists no oracle-bone or bronze example and only one small-seal example; this database absence is not proof that no earlier occurrence exists.

The alternative form 𣥦 is attributed by Shuowen to a shape with 止 instead of 足, but the evidence reviewed does not establish whether it is contemporary, earlier, or later than 跟. Classification as an earlier ancestor would be unsupported.

The proposed sound element is 艮, not a whole-graph loan. The phonological evidence supports a sound role; no separate depicted object, source word, or borrowed-word account is implicated by this analysis.

Heel-to-object-back and heel-to-follow extensions are plausible and described by the character database, but a complete dated sequence establishing the semantic links and first uses was not recovered. The object-back citation from 清稗類鈔 and later literary examples need edition-level dating.
The “跟 and 根 cognate” claim is attributed to Wang (1982) by Wiktionary; that cited argument was not inspected, and the relation should remain an attributed proposal rather than established fact.

Kotobank’s account that 艮 graphically signifies retreat through an evil-eye taboo conflicts in emphasis with the simple phonetic-component analysis and lacks corroboration among inspected paleographic sources. No glyph image was visually inspected.
